text: Big O; limits table; amortised and expected.

Time complexity (时间复杂度) counts how the number of basic steps grows with the input size n, ignoring constant factors: big O (大 O 记号) gives an upper bound, O(f(n)) means "at most c·f(n) steps for large n". Space complexity counts memory the same way. Judges run roughly 108 simple operations per second.

Read the limits first and work backwards to the complexity you need. Worst case is what matters on a judge; an "average O(n log n)" algorithm can be attacked by a bad input (quick sort without random pivots). n up to Feasible complexity Typical methods 10–12 O(n!) all permutations 20–25 O(2ⁿ · n) subsets, bitmask DP 100–500 O(n³) Floyd, interval DP 5 000 O(n²) simple DP, all pairs 10⁵–10⁶ O(n log n) sorting, segment trees, Dijkstra 10⁷–10⁸ O(n) prefix sums, two pointers, linear sieve 10¹⁸ O(log n) or O(√n) binary search, fast power, divisors
Amortised complexity (均摊) averages over a whole sequence of operations: a monotonic stack pushes and pops each element once, so n operations cost O(n) in total even though one step can pop many.
Expected complexity averages over the random choices of the algorithm (treap, randomised quick sort).
Unimodal functions; real and integer versions.

Ternary search (三分法) finds the maximum of a unimodal function: increasing, then decreasing. Pick m1 < m2 inside [l, r]. If f(m1) < f(m2), the maximum is not in [l, m1]; otherwise it is not in [m2, r]. Each step keeps 2/3 of the range: O(log n) steps.

Real numbers: loop a fixed number of times (100 iterations shrink any range below 10⁻¹⁵). Integers: stop when r − l < 3 and check the few remaining points. Ternary search needs strict monotonicity on each side; a flat part breaks it (the comparison cannot tell which side to drop).
P3382: the cubic x³ − 3x² − 3x + 1 rises then falls on [−0.9981, 0.5]; its maximum is at 1 − √2 ≈ −0.41421. The parabola −x² + 4x + 1 peaks at x = 2.
Integer version: while (r − l > 2) { m1 = l + (r − l)/3; m2 = r − (r − l)/3; … } then try l … r directly. Binary search on the slope (compare f(m) with f(m + 1)) is an equivalent integer trick.

Independence + exchange; jobs with deadlines.

A matroid (拟阵) is a family of "independent" sets with two rules: (1) every subset of an independent set is independent; (2) exchange: if A, B are independent and |A| < |B|, some element of B can be added to A keeping it independent. On a matroid, the greedy algorithm "take elements by decreasing weight, keep each one that stays independent" finds the maximum-weight independent set.

Examples: forests of a graph (Kruskal, 进阶篇第11章), linearly independent vectors (linear basis, 第11章), and sets of unit jobs that can all meet their deadlines. Recognising a matroid tells you greedy is provably optimal, no exchange argument needed each time.

Unit-time jobs with deadlines and profits: a set is independent when all its jobs can be scheduled before their deadlines. Greedy by profit, placing each job in the latest free slot (found with a DSU), is optimal.
Checked against Python trying every subset.
When the problem is not a matroid (e.g. jobs with different lengths, or a knapsack), greedy by weight can fail; then DP is needed.

Key points to memorise
1. O(f(n)): growth up to a constant; ~10⁸ simple steps per second.
2. Read n first: 20 → 2ⁿ, 500 → n³, 5000 → n², 10⁶ → n log n.
3. Ternary: compare f(m1), f(m2), drop a third; needs strict unimodality.
4. Real: fixed 100 iterations. Integer: stop at r − l < 3, test the rest.
5. kD difference: 2^k corners with sign (−1)^(far coordinates); rebuild axis by axis.
6. Matroid: hereditary + exchange ⇒ greedy by weight is optimal.
